video_metadata.working_title: MASSACHUSETTS 1964 Cold Case: Killer Identified After 49 Years — Justice for Mary Sullivan
video_metadata.topic_one_sentence: Nineteen-year-old Mary Sullivan was raped and strangled in her new Beacon Hill apartment on January 4, 1964, the last killing attributed to the Boston Strangler; Albert DeSalvo confessed but was never tried, was killed in prison in 1973, and only in July 2013 did familial Y-STR DNA from a nephew's discarded water bottle, followed by the exhumation of DeSalvo's remains, link him to her murder with odds quoted at one in 220 billion, while his responsibility for the other killings remains debated.
video_metadata.primary_emotion_to_evoke: grief turning into the bittersweet relief of a partial answer, with lingering unease about the other women

protagonist._instructions: The main character of your story - can be hero, villain, or antihero. Fill with verified facts only.
protagonist.full_name: Mary Sullivan (victim, the heart of the story); Albert Henry DeSalvo (the man the DNA identified)
protagonist.age_at_time_of_events: Mary Sullivan: 19 in January 1964. Albert DeSalvo: born September 3, 1931, so 32 in January 1964; 42 when he was killed in November 1973.
protagonist.occupation_or_status: Mary: a young woman from Cape Cod who had just moved to Boston. DeSalvo: married father of two, worked odd jobs/handyman work and construction-type labour (background; see notes); serving a life sentence for unrelated sexual assaults and robberies at his death; never charged with or convicted of any murder.
protagonist.location: 44A Charles Street, Beacon Hill, Boston, Massachusetts
protagonist.physical_description: Not used; real archival photo of Mary only.
protagonist.background_brief: Mary grew up on Cape Cod in an Irish Catholic family; her younger sister Diane, then 17, was her best friend. She moved into a third-floor apartment on Charles Street shared by three young women only days before she was killed (sources say between one and four days).
protagonist.psychological_profile: Not applicable to the victim. DeSalvo: con man and sexual predator by his record ('Measuring Man', 'Green Man'); Bridgewater psychiatrist Dr. Ames Robey reportedly doubted he was capable of homicide (per Casey Sherman, 2025).
protagonist.mundane_humanizing_detail: For her nephew Casey Sherman, Mary was a portrait on the mantel at home; his mother said they had planned to live their lives together.

collective_victims_if_applicable.group_description: Women killed in the Boston area between June 1962 and January 1964 whose murders were attributed to the 'Boston Strangler'
collective_victims_if_applicable.total_number_affected: 11 on the 'official' list; 13 counting two further killings DeSalvo also confessed to. Names usually listed: Anna Slesers (June 14, 1962), Mary Mullen (June 28, 1962), Nina Nichols (June 30, 1962), Helen Blake (June 30, 1962), Ida Irga (August 19, 1962), Jane Sullivan (August 20/21, 1962), Sophie Clark (December 5, 1962), Patricia Bissette (December 31, 1962), Mary Brown (March 1963), Beverly Samans (May 6, 1963), Evelyn Corbin (September 8/9, 1963), Joann Graff (November 23, 1963), Mary Sullivan (January 4, 1964).
collective_victims_if_applicable.range_of_impacts: Victims ranged in age from 85 to 19; most were sexually assaulted and strangled in their own homes; DNA evidence links DeSalvo only to Mary Sullivan.

supporting_characters._instructions: Investigators, accomplices, witnesses, family members - anyone who plays a significant role.

characters.name: Casey Sherman
characters.role_in_story: Mary's nephew (son of her sister Diane), journalist and author of 'A Rose for Mary' (2003)
characters.key_actions_they_took: Pushed for re-examination; involved in the 2000-2001 exhumations and private testing; in 2013 accepted the DNA result; in November 2025 hosted Oxygen's 'The Boston Strangler: Unheard Confession' and said he doubts DeSalvo was the Strangler
characters.notable_quotes: 'This is now full justice for my aunt, Mary Sullivan.' (2013) [5][21]; 'I only go where the evidence leads.' (2013) [21]; 'I've lived with Mary's memory every day, my whole life.' (2013, AP) [21]

characters.name: Daniel F. Conley
characters.key_actions_they_took: Announced the familial match on July 11, 2013, sought the exhumation, announced the confirmatory match on July 19, 2013; stressed the evidence applied only to the Sullivan case
characters.notable_quotes: Described the result as a 'familial match' (July 11, 2013) [6]

characters.name: Martha Coakley
characters.notable_quotes: Said the finding 'leaves no doubt that Albert DeSalvo was responsible for the brutal murder of Mary Sullivan' and that he was 'most likely' responsible for the other killings [3][4]

characters.name: Edward F. Davis
characters.key_actions_they_took: Joint announcements; his department's cold case squad ran the test

characters.name: Boston Police Department cold case squad
characters.key_actions_they_took: Used NIJ cold-case grant funding to compare the preserved crime-scene evidence with DNA from a DeSalvo nephew; an officer followed the nephew and collected a discarded water bottle

characters.name: James E. Starrs
characters.role_in_story: George Washington University professor of forensic science
characters.key_actions_they_took: Led the private team that exhumed DeSalvo in October 2001 and in December 2001 announced that DNA they found did not match him
characters.notable_quotes: 'We have found evidence and the evidence does not and cannot be associated with Albert DeSalvo.' [11]

characters.name: Elaine Whitfield Sharp
characters.key_actions_they_took: Objected to the covert collection of the nephew's DNA; disputed the 2013 conclusion
characters.notable_quotes: Objected that police would 'sneakily, creepily, take his water bottle and take his DNA' [6]

characters.name: Edward W. Brooke
characters.key_actions_they_took: Created the Special Division of Crime Research and Detection ('Strangler Bureau') led by Assistant AG John S. Bottomly; approved involvement of psychic Peter Hurkos

characters.name: John S. Bottomly
characters.role_in_story: Assistant AG heading the Strangler Bureau
characters.key_actions_they_took: Led the task force; appointment controversial because of his lack of criminal-law experience; took DeSalvo's 1965 confession statements (background)

characters.name: F. Lee Bailey
characters.key_actions_they_took: Took DeSalvo as a client after George Nassar told him of DeSalvo's claims; his client confessed in 1965 but was never tried for the murders

characters.name: George Nassar
characters.role_in_story: Fellow inmate at Bridgewater State Hospital
characters.key_actions_they_took: Told his attorney F. Lee Bailey that DeSalvo had confessed to him; named by some writers as an alternative suspect (no charges)

cold_open_material._instructions: The most dramatic moment of your story - this will be your hook.

the_moment.what_is_happening: A 19-year-old who has just moved from Cape Cod to the city is killed in her new apartment days after arriving
the_moment.what_makes_it_shocking: Boston had lived with a serial strangler for 19 months; she was the last victim
the_moment.ironic_twist: The man who confessed was never tried; his confession was doubted for decades, even by Mary's own family, and the answer came 49 years later from a water bottle thrown away by his nephew

cold_open_material.central_mystery_question: Did the man who confessed actually kill Mary Sullivan, and what does that tell us about the other women

the_method._instructions: How did the protagonist do what they did? Technical details that can be explained to a general audience.
the_method.technique_name: Familial Y-STR DNA comparison with covert discarded sample, followed by exhumation and direct confirmatory DNA testing
step_by_step_explanation: Seminal fluid from Mary's body and from a blanket at the scene had been preserved by Boston police for nearly 50 years
Analysts developed a Y-chromosome (Y-STR) profile from it
Because the Y chromosome passes almost unchanged from father to son, all men in a paternal line share it
An investigator collected a water bottle discarded by a DeSalvo nephew; his Y-STR profile matched the crime scene, excluding about 99.9 percent of men
A Y-STR match points to a family line, not an individual, so authorities obtained court approval to exhume DeSalvo
DNA from a femur and three teeth was compared directly; a nationally recognized lab reported a match with odds of one in 220 billion
the_method.why_it_worked: Evidence had been preserved; Y-STR testing works on male DNA even when mixed with female DNA; a paternal relative was available

technical_terms_to_explain.simple_explanation: A genetic surname: markers on the Y chromosome shared by a man, his father, brothers, sons and paternal nephews
The sample does not name a man, it names a family
A direct sample from the person himself, here from bone and teeth

the_method.scale_of_operation: One case out of 11-13; officials said there was not enough testable DNA in the other cases

systemic_failure._instructions: What institution, system, or authority failed to prevent this?
systemic_failure.institution_that_failed: A fragmented investigation across many police jurisdictions and a state task force; a legal system that never tested the confession
systemic_failure.why_they_failed: No forensic method could link a suspect in 1964; jurisdictions divided; DeSalvo's confession was never brought before a jury
specific_incompetence_examples: The Strangler Bureau was led by an Assistant AG criticized for lack of criminal-law experience [16]
Involvement of psychic Peter Hurkos damaged the Bureau's credibility; his suspect had no evidence against him [16]
DeSalvo was never charged with any murder; he received life for the Green Man crimes instead [13]
He was killed in 1973; the killer was never identified [13]
systemic_failure.ironic_details_about_the_failure: The evidence that answered the question had been in police storage the whole time; private tests in 2001 pointed the other way, and authorities later called that evidence questionable [22]

the_investigation.investigating_agency: Boston Police Department cold case squad, Suffolk County DA's office, Massachusetts AG's office
the_investigation.when_investigation_began: January 1964; cold case work funded by NIJ grants in 2009 and 2012
the_investigation.initial_wrong_assumptions: Many investigators and writers doubted a single killer; DeSalvo's confession was believed by some and doubted by others
the_investigation.key_breakthrough: Nephew's discarded water bottle gives a familial Y-STR match
the_investigation.the_fatal_mistake: Not applicable (DeSalvo was dead); the nephew's discarded bottle provided the lead
the_investigation.how_long_until_caught: Identified 49 years after the murder (January 1964 to July 2013); never tried

the_confrontation._instructions: The arrest, raid, or climactic moment when everything collapses.
the_confrontation.location: Puritan Lawn Memorial Park, Peabody; Office of the Chief Medical Examiner, Boston
the_confrontation.scene_description: Court-approved exhumation of DeSalvo's remains for confirmatory DNA testing
the_confrontation.protagonist_reaction: DeSalvo had been dead since 1973; his family's lawyer disputed the conclusion
the_confrontation.ironic_or_absurd_details: DeSalvo's grave had already been opened once, in 2001, by his own family trying to prove his innocence

charges_filed: DeSalvo: never charged with any Strangler murder
Convicted January 1967 of unrelated sexual assaults/robberies ('Green Man' cases), life sentence

victim_impact_statements.key_quote: This is now full justice for my aunt, Mary Sullivan.

legal_resolution.sentence_received: Life imprisonment for the Green Man crimes
legal_resolution.current_status: As of October 2026: DeSalvo dead since November 26, 1973, never convicted of any murder; authorities stated in 2013 the DNA identifies him as the source of the Sullivan evidence; no DNA link to the other killings; his responsibility for them remains debated (Sherman's 2025 documentary disputes it). No search found any new official development after 2013.

details: The man who confessed to being the Boston Strangler was never charged with a single murder
Mary's own nephew spent years arguing DeSalvo was innocent of her murder, then accepted the 2013 DNA, then in 2025 again voiced doubts about DeSalvo as the Strangler
DeSalvo's grave was opened twice: in 2001 by his family to clear him, in 2013 by prosecutors to confirm the link
The answer came from a nephew who had done nothing wrong and threw away a water bottle

universal_stakes.why_this_matters_to_viewer: A confession is not proof; evidence preserved for decades can answer questions no one could answer at the time
universal_stakes.how_this_could_happen_to_them: Mary was a young woman starting her life in a new city
universal_stakes.lesson_or_warning: Keep the evidence; test the confession; separate what is proven from what is assumed
universal_stakes.current_relevance: Familial DNA and covert discarded samples are now routine in cold cases, and still debated on privacy grounds
